about: MQTT has fourteen control packet types and six of them are described here: CONNECT, CONNACK,
SUBSCRIBE, SUBACK, PINGREQ and PINGRESP. Each is its own message, because each is its own format —
§3.1 through §3.14 give them one section apiece — and each is a single path from the first octet to
the last with nothing to decide along the way.
WHICH ONE THIS IS, IS SOMETHING THE MESSAGE SAYS. There is no caller to ask on the way in and nothing
has been read yet, so the reading looks: `identifies` lays a path to the field that discriminates,
reads it from a copy of the position, and matches it against the key on each way on. Nothing is
consumed, so the message that gets chosen reads its own fixed header from its own first octet — which
is why no message here has to know it has siblings, or that something looked before choosing it.
Going out the same fork is decided the ordinary way, by what the caller asked for. Two directions,
two sources for one fact, and the fact is the same one: the packet type.
WHAT IS SHARED AND WHAT IS NOT. A concept common to several messages is one node — the Packet
Identifier a SUBSCRIBE allocates and its SUBACK echoes is one input, named once, read by both. What is
NOT shared is a field whose legal values differ: a CONNECT's packet type is the constant 1 and a
CONNACK's is the constant 2, so they are two nodes that happen to be instances of one idea. The idea
itself is a node as well, and it is the one the reading consults.
STRINGS. §1.5.3 defines one shape — two octets of length, then that many octets — and every string in
the protocol is an instance of it. Each is a set holding its own count and its own octets, so a
Client Identifier and a Will Topic share a shape and nothing else.
§2.2.1: the high four bits of the first octet. This is the concept — 'which control packet is this' —
as opposed to any one message's declaration that it is a particular one.
It is read from a copy of the reader's position and consumed from nothing. Whichever message it picks
then reads the same four bits again as the first thing in its own fixed header, which costs one nibble
of work and buys every message the right to be described as though it were the only one.

nodes.purpose: Which control packet to write: 1 CONNECT, 2 CONNACK, 8 SUBSCRIBE, 9 SUBACK, 12 PINGREQ, 13 PINGRESP.

about: Where a reading may stop, and the only place. Two of the messages here read round a loop until the
octets run out, and a loop that has run out is indistinguishable from one that was cut short unless
something says which endings were legal.

nodes.because: §2.2.1 Table 2.1 assigns the fourteen control packet types; six are described here.

about: §3.1 — the first packet a client sends, and the only one legal before a CONNACK has come back.
Most of it is conditional on one octet. The connect flags say whether there is a will, a user name and
a password, and in the corpus capture that decides 114 of the packet's 146 octets. Each of those parts
is an ordinary optional step whose presence reads the flag that governs it — one fact, so a flag and
the part it announces cannot disagree.

nodes.about: §2.2.2: reserved for this packet type, and the only legal value is 0000.

about: §2.2.3. Seven bits of value per octet with the top bit meaning 'another follows', least
significant group first — so `8f 01` is 15 + 1×128 = 143 and `02` is 2. The width of the
field is a function of the value it carries, which is why it is a form rather than a width.
Non-minimal chains are refused: `8f 80 00` also arrives at 15, and accepting it would give
one value two encodings and make a re-write differ from what was read.

about: §3.8 — one or more topic filters, each with the quality of service the client is asking for.
HOW MANY THERE ARE IS NOWHERE IN THE PACKET. §3.8.3 says the payload holds a list and the
remaining length says where it ends, which is a fact about a message rather than about MQTT.
So going out the payload is written once per item of the list it requires, and coming in the
reading goes round until the octets run out. Neither direction has a count and neither wants
one — a count in the description would have to be right about a number the protocol never
states.

nodes.about: §3.8.1: this one is not reserved — it is mandated to be 0010, and a server must close the connection on anything else.

about: §2.3.1. The token the SUBACK echoes, which is how an answer is matched to what it answers.
Its own node rather than one shared with the SUBACK's, because a field is a place in a message and
these are two places in two messages. What they share is a VALUE, and the value has a node of its own
— one input, read by both — which is where sameness belongs.

nodes.about: §3.8.3.1: the maximum QoS the client is asking the server to send at. The top six bits are reserved.

nodes.purpose: §2.3.1: a non-zero 16-bit token, unique among the messages currently in flight.
What to subscribe to: each item says its `filter` (octets) and its `qos`.

nodes.about: §4.7: a topic name with wildcards allowed — `+` for one level, `#` for the rest.

about: Only the reading comes here. Going out the payload knows how many times to go round — it is the
length of the list — and coming in there is no such number anywhere, so what says whether another
follows is whether there are octets left.
§3.9 — one return code per topic filter of the SUBSCRIBE it answers, in the same order.
The count is positional and appears nowhere: §3.9.3 says the number of return codes MUST match the
number of filters, so the only way to know how many there are is to read until the packet ends. A
return code is not simply an acceptance — 0x80 refuses a subscription outright, and a code lower than
what was asked for is the server granting less than the client requested.
